title: You read Genesis 22 and something inside you recoils.
paragraphs: You read Genesis 22 and something inside you recoils.
Why would God ask a father to sacrifice his son?
Not just any son. The promised son. The miracle child. The covenant carrier.
At first glance, it feels cruel. Contradictory. Almost pagan.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
Genesis 22 is not ultimately about Isaac dying.
It is about God revealing something humanity could not yet fully see.
A Father who would one day give His own Son.
And Abraham, trembling on Mount Moriah, was walking inside a prophetic shadow of the Gospel itself.
The story begins in Genesis 22:1:
“After these things God tested Abraham…”
The Hebrew word used here is:
נִסָּה (nissah)
It means “to test,” “to prove,” or “to reveal what is inside.”
This is critically important.
The text does not say God tempted Abraham to evil.
Scripture is clear:

“God cannot be tempted with evil, and He himself tempts no one.”
— James 1:13
The Hebrew context reveals this was a covenant test of faith and trust, not divine cruelty.
God was exposing whether Abraham trusted the promise more than the Promiser.
And honestly…
That question still confronts people today.

Do you love God…
or merely what He gives you?
God had already promised Abraham:

“Through Isaac shall your offspring be named.”
— Genesis 21:12
So when God says in Genesis 22:2:
“Take your son, your only son Isaac, whom you love…”
the wording is intentional.
The Hebrew phrase is devastatingly personal:

קַח־נָא אֶת־בִּנְךָ אֶת־יְחִידְךָ אֲשֶׁר־אָהַבְתָּ
(Qach-na eth-bincha eth-yechidcha asher-ahavta)
“Take now your son, your unique son, whom you love.”
“Yechidcha” (יְחִידְךָ) means unique, beloved, one-and-only covenant son.
This language echoes forward prophetically into the New Testament.
Because centuries later Scripture says:

“For God so loved the world, that He gave His only begotten Son…”
— John 3:16
In Greek:
μονογενῆ υἱόν (monogenē huion)
“Only unique Son.”
The parallels are impossible to ignore.

A father.
A beloved son.
A journey toward sacrifice.
Wood carried upward.
A mountain chosen by God.
This is not random history.
This is prophetic architecture.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior, this moment becomes one of the clearest Gospel foreshadowings in all Scripture.
Then comes one of the most haunting moments in the Bible.
Isaac asks:

“Behold, the fire and the wood, but where is the lamb?”
— Genesis 22:7
Abraham responds:

“God will provide for Himself the lamb.”
— Genesis 22:8
In Hebrew:

אֱלֹהִים יִרְאֶה־לּוֹ הַשֶּׂה
(Elohim yir’eh-lo haseh)
Literally:
“God Himself will see/provide the lamb.”
The Hebrew word יִרְאֶה (yir’eh) comes from רָאָה (ra’ah) — “to see.”
In ancient Hebrew thought, God “seeing” meant God acting in provision.
This becomes the name:

יְהוָה יִרְאֶה
(YHWH Yireh / Jehovah Jireh)
“The LORD will provide.”
But notice carefully.
Isaac asked for a lamb.
Genesis says God provided a ram.
The lamb was still coming.
Read that again.
The lamb was still coming.
Two thousand years later, near the same region of Moriah, another Son would carry wood up a hill.
Not Isaac.
Jesus.
And this time the Father would not stop the sacrifice.
When John the Baptist saw Jesus, he declared:

“Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!”
— John 1:29
In Greek:

Ἴδε ὁ ἀμνὸς τοῦ Θεοῦ
(Ide ho amnos tou Theou)
“The Lamb of God.”
Genesis 22 was never merely about Abraham losing Isaac.
It was God unveiling redemption history.
But there’s another layer many overlook.
Abraham already believed Isaac would live again.
Hebrews 11:19 says:
“He considered that God was able even to raise him from the dead…”
The Greek word for “considered” is:
λογισάμενος (logisamenos)
Meaning reasoned, calculated, concluded logically.
Abraham was not acting irrationally.
He believed one of two things had to happen:
Either God would stop the sacrifice…
or God would resurrect Isaac.
Because God’s promise could not fail.
That changes everything.
Abraham trusted God beyond what he could emotionally understand.
And that is where many people struggle.
You want explanations before obedience.
You want clarity before surrender.
You want guarantees before trust.
But biblical faith often walks uphill carrying wood before it sees provision.
God saw Abraham’s heart.
God saw that Isaac had not become an idol.
God saw that Abraham trusted Him more than the blessing itself.
You knew this story was deeper than surface-level morality.
God saw it.
And hidden inside this account is one of the most misunderstood truths in Scripture:
God never ultimately desired human sacrifice.
In fact, later He strongly condemns pagan child sacrifice repeatedly:

“They burned their sons and daughters in the fire, which I did not command, nor did it enter my mind.”
— Jeremiah 7:31
So why the command?
Because God was revealing substitutionary atonement.
A substitute would die in the place of another.

The ram dies.
Isaac lives.
This becomes the theological backbone of the Gospel.

Jesus dies.
Sinners live.
That is why this story matters.
It is not about glorifying suffering.
It is about revealing salvation.
And maybe the most terrifying realization is this:
On Mount Moriah, Abraham was spared from giving his son.
But when humanity stood guilty in sin…
God did not spare His own Son.
Romans 8:32 says:
“He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all…”
In Greek:

ὃς γε τοῦ ἰδίου υἱοῦ οὐκ ἐφείσατο
(hos ge tou idiou huiou ouk epheisato)
“Who did not withhold His own Son.”
The language intentionally echoes Genesis 22.
The Gospel was always the destination.
Always.
The binding of Isaac — called the Aqedah (עֲקֵידָה) in Hebrew, meaning “binding” — points beyond itself to Christ.
Every thread leads there.

The wood.
The father.
The son.
The mountain.
The sacrifice.
The substitute.
The promise.
The resurrection imagery.
All of it.
Jesus stands at the center.
But here’s the part people avoid.
This story also confronts your own heart.
What sits on the altar above God?

Career?
Relationships?
Comfort?
Pride?
Secret sin?
Control?
Some people claim to follow God while negotiating permanent disobedience.
Abraham walked three days toward surrender.
Many people today will not walk three minutes toward obedience.
And still God calls.
Still God provides.
Still grace stands available through Jesus Christ.
Not through works.
Not through religion.
Not through self-improvement.
Through Christ alone.
Because the true horror is not that Abraham almost sacrificed Isaac.
The true horror is that sinners deserved judgment…
and God chose to place it upon Himself.
That is the Gospel.
That is why Genesis 22 exists.
And once you see it…
you cannot unsee it.
